edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' (e.g. K1-1) on every page instead of a bare page number at the right margin.

edits.quote: Find all the ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Put each way on a shape of its own.
edits.fix: The page shows seven outlines but only two shapes, and the small hexagon's two coverings are turns of each other. Say: 'Find all the ways to cover the small hexagon with blue blocks, one way on each copy. Then do the same for the long hexagon. Two ways are different if any block is in a different place.'

edits.quote: Page 7: four more copies of the Problem 6 hexagon with no text; P6 says 'cover this shape'
edits.fix: In P6 write 'Put each way on a shape of its own (this page and the next)' so the adult and child know page 7 belongs to P6.

k-1.summary: Six concrete, actual-size block problems bring both kernels to K-1 level: possible and impossible shapes (including the even-area trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down triangles), fewest greens, finding all coverings of three hexagons (2, 3 and 6 ways), fewest blocks (answers 3, 3, 4) and a placement game (first, second, first, first, second). Every board and answer checks out, and there is enough work to fill the session. Only small edits are needed: make clear which outlines in P3 are copies of one shape and whether turned coverings count, label the continuation page, and fix the footer.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Find a rule that tells which places for the two green triangles work, and explain why your rule is right.
edits.fix: The rule is one up-triangle and one down-triangle, and all 144 such placements on this hexagon do work (checked). But proving that every such placement works is beyond grades 2-3. Ask children to find the rule and explain why the placements that fail can never work, and leave the 'always works' half with the adult.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side.
edits.fix: The bottom row of such a board has 19 small triangles, so 'along each side' can be miscounted. Say 'a triangle board whose sides are 10 small edges long' (and use the same wording in the P5 table labels).

grades-2-3.summary: This is a well-sequenced development of the colouring obstruction: possible and impossible boards (including the hourglass, which is balanced but cannot be tiled), fewest greens for sides 2-5 with a proof, generalising to sides 10 and 100, chevrons (never better, and worse for sides 2 and 3), designing a 20-triangle board that needs 6 greens (13 up / 7 down, the maximum, which fits the grid), and the two-green rule on the side-2 hexagon. All diagrams are correct and at actual size. Only light edits are needed: P7 asks for a sufficiency proof beyond the band, one wording ambiguity, and the footer.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: On the small boards below, draw all your coverings from Problem 1 again.
edits.fix: Recopying the six coverings is clerical padding. Have children draw the flip lines between their Problem 1 drawings (give P1's small boards room for this), or tell them to arrange the copies so that coverings one flip apart sit next to each other. Do not just say 'again'.

edits.quote: Explain why, whenever you make flips and end at the covering you started with, you have made an even number of flips.
edits.fix: This prints the answer to P4's 'Can you do it with 5 flips? With 7 flips?'. End P4 with 'Explain.' and drop the statement here, or ask it as a question: 'Can a round trip ever use an odd number of flips?'

edits.quote: Then find the fewest flips that change covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: The 'find the fewest' part repeats P3's E-F box (the answer is 8). Keep only: 'Explain why nobody can change covering E into covering F with fewer flips than you found.'

edits.quote: Draw them on the small hexagons below (25 side-2 hexagons with 0.3-inch triangles)
edits.fix: Drawing 20 coverings of 12 rhombi each on 0.3-inch triangles is cramped, clerical work. Let children record each covering by its pair of ribbons (add a ribbon list space) and keep fewer, larger hexagons for drawing.

grades-4-5.summary: This is a strong kernel-2 sequence: find the 6 coverings, build their flip graph (one farthest pair, 4 flips), find flip distances on the side-2 hexagon (A-B 3, C-D 4, E-F 8, all checked), study the parity of round trips, define ribbons (the LRRLR example is correct), and count the 20 coverings of the 1-3-3 and 2-2-2 boards. The diagrams and claims are correct, and the definitions are lean but complete. The edits remove clerical recopying in P2 and P8, stop P6 from printing P4's discovery, cut P6's repeat of P3's E-F task, and fix the footer.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 sequence takes the colouring obstruction from hands-on impossible boards through lower-bound proofs, generalisation, chevrons, board design and a two-hole rule, with every board correct and at actual size.
overall.weakest: Grades 4-5 asks for clerical re-drawing (all P1 coverings again in P2, and 20 full coverings on tiny hexagons in P8), and its P6 prints the parity result that P4 asks children to discover.
